lead: A transmission line is not a wire but a distributed circuit: every metre adds series resistance and inductance and shunt conductance and capacitance. Written per metre, these four numbers are the primary constants. Put them into the telegrapher's equations and the solution describes two waves travelling in opposite directions, with one characteristic impedance Z0 and one propagation constant γ. From γ come attenuation, phase constant, wavelength and velocity. Every RF design starts here: a 50 Ω cable, a microstrip trace on a printed circuit board, a coaxial feed to an antenna.
prereq: You need: Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws, phasor notation with angular frequency ω = 2πf, complex numbers in rectangular and polar form, and the physical idea that a wire stores magnetic energy while two nearby conductors store electric energy.

blocks.text: A transmission line carries a signal from one point to another and always has a return path, so it is at least two conductors: the inner and outer of a coaxial cable, a microstrip trace over a ground plane, or the two wires of a twisted pair.

At low frequency you can pretend the whole line is one resistor and ignore the rest. At radio and microwave frequency the line is long compared with the wavelength, and voltage and current change from centimetre to centimetre. So we describe a short slice of length Δz and let Δz shrink to zero.
Some syllabi call R, L, G and C the primary line constants. All four are per metre. A 20 m cable has total series inductance 20L, not L. Keep them per metre until the final answer.

sections.h3: Telegrapher's equations and the general solution

blocks.text: Take a slice Δz, apply Kirchhoff's voltage law round the series path and Kirchhoff's current law at the shunt node, divide by Δz and let Δz → 0. In phasor form:
dV/dz = −(R + jωL) I        dI/dz = −(G + jωC) V
blocks.where: V and I are phasor voltage and current at distance z from the sending end, in V and A; R, L, G, C are per-metre constants; ω = 2πf rad/s; j is the imaginary unit.

blocks.text: Differentiate the first equation and substitute the second. The voltage obeys d²V/dz² = γ²V, with

blocks.where: γ is the propagation constant; α is the attenuation constant in nepers per metre (Np/m); β is the phase constant in radians per metre (rad/m).
V⁺ is the forward wave amplitude at z = 0, V⁻ is the backward wave amplitude, both in V.

blocks.text: The matching current is I(z) = (V⁺/Z0)e^(−γz) − (V⁻/Z0)e^(γz), with

blocks.where: Z0 is the characteristic impedance in ohms; it is the ratio V⁺/I⁺ of a single forward wave.

blocks.text: The minus sign on the backward current is the step most often lost in exams. γ and Z0 are called secondary constants because they follow from R, L, G, C rather than being measured separately.
Set R = G = 0. Then the constants become simple:
Z0 = √(L/C)    β = ω√(LC)    vp = 1/√(LC)    λ = 2π/β = vp/f
blocks.where: Z0 in Ω is now purely real; β in rad/m; vp is the phase velocity in m/s; λ in m; f in Hz.

blocks.text: vp is set by the dielectric, not by free space. For plastic-insulated cable it is often about two-thirds of c, where c = 3×10⁸ m/s. A common error is to assume vp = c.

With R and G present, Z0 is complex and α > 0. A pulse contains many frequencies; if α and β vary with frequency, the components are attenuated unequally and travel at different speeds, so the pulse arrives smeared. The line is distortionless when R/L = G/C. Then Z0 = √(L/C) is real again, β = ω√(LC), and α = R√(C/L) = G√(L/C) is flat in frequency, so every component is attenuated by the same factor. Real cables rarely satisfy this, so telephone lines add series inductors (loading coils) to raise L and bring R/L down towards G/C.

An infinite line has no backward wave, so its input impedance is exactly Z0. A finite line ended in Z0 behaves the same; any other load creates a reflected wave, which is the subject of 1.2, and the impedance seen at the input is covered in 1.3.
Forward-wave power is P⁺ = |V⁺|²/(2Z0) W for real Z0. A line of length l and attenuation α delivers a fraction e^(−2αl) of that power, so the transmission efficiency is η = e^(−2αl).

figure.caption: The four per-metre constants feed the telegrapher's equations; their solution gives Z0 and γ, and β then fixes wavelength and velocity. Notice that no load appears anywhere: everything here is a property of the line alone.

spec.title: From primary to secondary constants
spec.aria: Primary line constants feed the telegrapher equations, whose solution gives Z0, γ, wavelength and velocity.

examples.question: A lossless coaxial line has L = 0.25 μH/m and C = 100 pF/m. (a) Find Z0. (b) Find the phase velocity. (c) Find the wavelength at 100 MHz. (d) How long does a signal take to travel 3 m of this line?
steps: Convert to SI: L = 0.25 μH/m = 2.5×10⁻⁷ H/m; C = 100 pF/m = 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ F/m.
(c) λ = vp/f = 2×10⁸ / 1×10⁸ = 2 m. Check: β = 2π/λ = π rad/m, and ω = 2π×10⁸ rad/s, so ω/β = 2×10⁸ m/s.
examples.answer: Z0 = 50 Ω, vp = 2×10⁸ m/s, λ = 2 m at 100 MHz, and a 3 m delay of 15 ns.

C = 100e-12
Z0 = (L / C) ** 0.5

traps: Per metre versus total: putting the total L of a 20 m cable into √(L/C) gives an answer wrong by √20. Convert to per-metre values first.
Using free-space c for vp. On a line vp = 1/√(LC) is fixed by the dielectric and is normally below c.
Writing Z0 = √(L/C) when R and G are not zero. That formula is the lossless line only; the general Z0 is complex.
Dropping the minus sign in dV/dz = −(R + jωL)I, or in the backward current term, which then makes the two waves add instead of travelling opposite ways.
Thinking Z0 can be measured with an ohmmeter on an open cable. The meter reads the DC open-circuit resistance, which is nearly infinite, not Z0.

quiz.q: Name the four primary line constants, with units, and say where each comes from.
quiz.a: R (Ω/m) from metal resistance, L (H/m) from the magnetic field, G (S/m) from dielectric leakage, C (F/m) from the electric field between conductors.

quiz.q: Why is Z0 real for a lossless line but complex when R and G are present?
quiz.a: Z0 = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)). With R = G = 0 the jω factors cancel, leaving √(L/C), a real number, so voltage and current are in phase. With R and G present the ratio has an angle, so Z0 is complex and there is a small phase shift between V and I on a single wave.

quiz.q: A lossless line has L = 400 nH/m and C = 100 pF/m. Find Z0 and vp.
A line has α = 0.02 Np/m and is 50 m long. Find the transmission efficiency and the loss in dB.
Why does a line with R and G present distort a pulse, and what condition removes the distortion?
quiz.a: Each frequency component sees a different α and a different β, so the components are attenuated unequally and arrive with different delays; the pulse spreads. If R/L = G/C, then α = R√(C/L) is independent of frequency and β = ω√(LC) is linear in ω, so the shape is preserved and only the amplitude falls.

quiz.q: A cable has R/L greater than G/C. Are the high-frequency components of a pulse attenuated more or less than the low ones, and how do loading coils help?
quiz.a: When R/L > G/C the attenuation rises with frequency, so the high-frequency components are attenuated more and the pulse edges round off. Loading coils add series inductance, which raises L and lowers R/L towards G/C, flattening α against frequency.

quiz.q: Write the telegrapher's equations in phasor form and define every symbol.
quiz.a: dV/dz = −(R + jωL)I and dI/dz = −(G + jωC)V; V, I are phasor voltage (V) and current (A) at distance z (m); R, L, G, C are per-metre constants; ω = 2πf in rad/s.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every high-speed link, from a USB cable to a 5G millimetre-wave feed to the trace between a SerDes chip and a connector, is designed with these same equations; the loss per metre plotted against frequency is the insertion-loss curve on a datasheet. Channel simulators solve the telegrapher's equations with R and L made frequency-dependent by the skin effect, and G and C made frequency-dependent by dielectric loss, then produce eye diagrams. On-chip, the same model becomes the RC ladder used for interconnect delay. Search 'telegrapher's equations', 'distortionless line', 'insertion loss dB per inch' and 'eye diagram'.
